skill: Infective endocarditis and acute valve failure
stem: A 60-year-old with untreated Streptococcus aureus bacteraemia develops sudden severe dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema. A new early diastolic murmur is heard and echocardiography shows flail aortic cusp with severe regurgitation and vegetation. BP is 86/46 mmHg.
ask: Which treatment plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Continue IV antibiotics alone for six weeks before considering surgery.
Treat with diuretics only and delay valve assessment until infection clears.
Activate urgent cardiothoracic surgical/endocarditis team while providing resuscitation and IV targeted antibiotics.
Give high-dose beta blocker to prolong diastole and increase forward output.
Perform routine treadmill stress echo to confirm haemodynamic significance.
explanations: Acute severe aortic regurgitation with shock is a surgical emergency; antimicrobials alone are insufficient.
Decongestion may help temporarily but cannot repair acute valve destruction.
Correct: destructive endocarditis with acute heart failure is an urgent indication for surgical assessment.
Slow HR can worsen regurgitant volume in acute severe AR and shock.
Severe acute valve failure and shock make stress testing dangerous.
pearl: In endocarditis, acute severe regurgitation/heart failure is an emergency surgical indication—not a situation to wait for antibiotic completion.
pivot: Stable uncomplicated native-valve endocarditis may be treated medically with serial echo and microbiology.

steps: Stabilise
ABCDE, oxygen/ventilation and critical-care haemodynamic support.
Treat infection
Blood cultures if not already, organism-directed IV antibiotics and monitor bacteremia.
Operate early
Urgent cardiac surgery for valve destruction, periannular complications or uncontrolled infection.
Monitor
Renal, embolic, conduction-system and haemodynamic complications.
management.safety: A new AV block in aortic endocarditis suggests periannular abscess.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 44-year-old with metastatic lung cancer develops severe dyspnoea, HR 130/min, BP 78/48 mmHg, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. Bedside echo shows large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate intervention?
options: Give aggressive IV diuretics to relieve venous congestion.
Provide temporising support and urgent ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis by an experienced operator.
Give nitrates to lower JVP before drainage.
Schedule elective pericardial biopsy next month and monitor.
Begin high-dose NSAIDs as sole therapy for suspected viral pericarditis.
explanations: Reducing preload worsens tamponade physiology.
Correct: haemodynamic tamponade requires prompt drainage and resuscitation.
Vasodilation reduces perfusion in obstructive shock.
The patient is in shock requiring immediate decompression.
Large malignant tamponade cannot be resolved quickly with anti-inflammatories.
pearl: Tamponade causes obstructive shock; pericardial drainage, not diuresis, reverses physiology.
pivot: A small asymptomatic effusion without chamber collapse is usually monitored/etiologically assessed.

steps: Recognise
ABC, ECG and echocardiographic haemodynamics, IV access and senior cardiac/ICU help.
Temporise
Judicious fluids if needed; avoid drugs that markedly decrease preload before definitive drainage.
Drain
Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis or surgical window if appropriate.
Treat cause
Investigate malignant/infective aetiology and recurrence prevention.
management.safety: Positive-pressure ventilation may worsen shock before tamponade is relieved.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 57-year-old taking loop diuretics develops weakness and palpitations. K is 2.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.42 mmol/L and ECG shows prominent U waves with ventricular ectopics. Kidney function is normal.
ask: Which immediate treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Give rapid undiluted IV potassium chloride bolus through peripheral cannula.
Provide monitored IV potassium replacement with magnesium correction and treatment of ongoing losses.
Give oral potassium alone and defer ECG monitoring.
Give IV insulin to shift potassium into cells.
Increase loop diuretic to remove excess sodium.
explanations: Undiluted IV KCl bolus may cause fatal arrhythmias and tissue injury.
Correct: life-threatening hypokalaemia with ECG changes requires carefully controlled parenteral correction.
Marked depletion with ventricular ectopy needs cardiac monitoring and faster controlled correction.
Insulin lowers serum potassium further.
More diuresis worsens potassium/magnesium loss.
pearl: Magnesium depletion makes hypokalaemia refractory until both are corrected.
pivot: Mild asymptomatic hypokalaemia can often be treated orally and medication-adjusted.

steps: Assess
Continuous ECG, acid-base, renal and magnesium values, identify diuretics/diarrhoea.
Replace
Monitored diluted IV KCl at protocol-approved rate/concentration and correct Mg.
Recheck
Frequent serum K/Mg and ECG, adjust for renal function.
Prevent
Modify causative medications and arrange follow-up electrolyte checks.
management.safety: Never administer IV potassium as undiluted push.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 32-year-old presents with gum bleeding, bruising and fatigue. FBC shows Hb 82 g/L, platelets 22 ×10^9/L and abnormal promyelocytes on film. INR 1.7, fibrinogen 0.7 g/L, D-dimer high. Molecular confirmation is pending.
ask: Which intervention is MOST appropriate before molecular confirmation?
options: Give ATRA promptly with haematology guidance while correcting coagulopathy.
Wait for cytogenetics before treating because ATRA is not time sensitive.
Start routine iron supplements and review blood counts in two weeks.
Perform lumbar puncture immediately to stage disease.
Give prophylactic anticoagulation alone to treat microvascular thrombosis.
explanations: Correct: suspected APL is a haematological emergency with early fatal DIC; ATRA should not wait for PML-RARA confirmation.
Delays can cause catastrophic bleeding from DIC.
Findings indicate acute leukaemia and consumptive coagulopathy, not isolated deficiency.
Severe thrombocytopenia and DIC make LP unsafe.
Primary priority is ATRA and coagulation support under specialist care.
pearl: APL is 'treat on suspicion': ATRA can rapidly reduce coagulopathy-driven early deaths.
pivot: Other AML subtypes need prompt specialist treatment, but APL is uniquely time-critical for empiric ATRA.

steps: Recognise
Urgent haematology call, bleeding assessment and film review.
Treat empirically
Start all-trans retinoic acid via haematology and send molecular testing.
Correct bleeding risk
Support platelets, fibrinogen and coagulation targets with blood products per APL pathway.
Monitor
DIC, differentiation syndrome, organ function and infection.
management.safety: Avoid invasive procedures until coagulopathy is controlled.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

skill: HIV opportunistic infection with low CD4
stem: A 37-year-old living with HIV, off antiretroviral therapy, has three weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough and fever. CD4 is 45 cells/µL, SpO2 87% room air, CXR shows bilateral diffuse interstitial opacities and LDH elevated.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial therapy?
options: Treat as pulmonary embolism using anticoagulation alone.
Give oral azithromycin monotherapy and discharge.
Begin high-dose co-trimoxazole and assess need for adjunct corticosteroids based on oxygenation.
Start antifungal fluconazole alone because HIV predisposes to all fungal lung infections.
Start ART as the only acute treatment and wait for immune reconstitution.
explanations: Subacute dry cough, immunosuppression and diffuse infiltrates strongly suggest Pneumocystis pneumonia.
Severe hypoxaemia needs inpatient PCP-directed therapy.
Correct: PCP with moderate/severe hypoxaemia may benefit from corticosteroids and TMP-SMX.
Fluconazole does not treat Pneumocystis.
ART is important but does not replace immediate pneumonia therapy.
pearl: Pneumocystis pneumonia causes subacute dyspnoea, dry cough and hypoxaemia disproportionate to examination in advanced HIV.
pivot: If CD4 higher and lobar consolidation with purulent sputum, bacterial CAP becomes more likely.

steps: Assess severity
ABG/SpO2, imaging, renal function, microbiologic PCR/staining and other infectious differential.
Treat now
TMP-SMX appropriate to severity; adjunct steroids when gas-exchange criteria met.
Support
Oxygen, inpatient monitoring and evaluate treatment response.
Coordinate ART
ID/HIV team to arrange appropriately timed ART initiation and prophylaxis.
management.safety: Sulfonamide reactions and renal/electrolyte effects require close monitoring.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 40-year-old with AIDS (CD4 28) has two weeks of headache, fever and blurred vision. LP opening pressure is 38 cm H₂O, CSF cryptococcal antigen positive and meningism mild. BP is stable.
options: Treat with oral fluconazole at low dose alone without addressing CSF pressure.
Begin antifungal induction and perform serial therapeutic lumbar punctures to reduce CSF pressure.
Give routine IV dexamethasone to every patient with cryptococcal meningitis.
Start ART immediately before antifungal treatment to clear infection faster.
Place a blind ventricular drain without considering serial LP or clinical criteria.
explanations: High fungal burden and elevated intracranial pressure need induction therapy and therapeutic drainage.
Correct: cryptococcal meningitis requires appropriate amphotericin-based induction and active pressure management.
Routine steroids are generally not indicated and can harm in HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis.
Immediate ART can increase mortality in cryptococcal meningitis because of severe IRIS; timing is specialist-directed.
CSF diversion is selective for refractory raised ICP.
pearl: Raised CSF opening pressure is a major cause of cryptococcal morbidity; serial therapeutic LP saves lives.
pivot: Tuberculous meningitis has a different drug regimen and may include corticosteroid therapy.

steps: Treat fungus
ID-led amphotericin-based induction with flucytosine when appropriate, then consolidation/maintenance.
Relieve pressure
Measure opening pressure and repeat therapeutic LPs to target symptoms/pressure.
Monitor
Renal, electrolyte, marrow and hearing issues from antifungal therapy.
Plan ART timing
Discuss delayed initiation under HIV/ID guidance to balance IRIS risk.
management.safety: Do not routinely use acetazolamide or mannitol for cryptococcal raised ICP.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

skill: Pulmonary hypertension and connective tissue disease
stem: A 35-year-old with systemic sclerosis reports progressive exertional syncope and dyspnoea. Echo estimates high pulmonary artery systolic pressure with right-heart enlargement. Spirometry is near normal and no large PE is found.
ask: What is the BEST next diagnostic step before disease-specific PAH therapy?
options: Start maximal pulmonary vasodilator therapy solely from echocardiographic estimate.
Arrange specialist right-heart catheterisation to define pre- versus post-capillary physiology.
Treat with empirical high-dose diuretics without haemodynamic assessment.
Perform routine coronary angiography as the only test.
Discharge because near-normal spirometry excludes serious lung vascular disease.
explanations: Echo estimates probability but right heart catheterisation is required for haemodynamic confirmation/classification.
Correct: catheterisation confirms pulmonary hypertension and guides therapy.
Diuresis may reduce congestion but cannot establish PH subtype.
Coronary disease may be considered separately, but PH haemodynamics are central.
PAH can exist with relatively preserved spirometry.
pearl: Pulmonary hypertension is not a single disease: pre- and post-capillary types demand different management.
pivot: If left ventricular filling pressures are elevated, group 2 PH treatment focuses on the heart rather than PAH drugs.

steps: Recognise
Syncope/right-heart failure signs; urgent PH centre referral.
Characterise
Echo, BNP, PFT/DLCO, V/Q for chronic thromboembolic disease and right-heart catheterisation.
Treat subtype
PAH-specific therapy only after specialist haemodynamic diagnosis and risk stratification.
Support
Oxygen when hypoxaemic, vaccination and careful congestion management.
management.safety: Certain systemic sclerosis PH patients deteriorate quickly; exertional syncope is a high-risk sign.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 71-year-old has four weeks of progressive painless jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. She has lost 6 kg, has a palpable nontender gallbladder and ultrasound reveals dilated intra-/extrahepatic bile ducts.
ask: Which investigation is MOST appropriate next?
options: Perform urgent pancreatic-protocol CT with specialist hepatopancreatobiliary referral to define obstruction and stage possible malignancy.
Prescribe oral antibiotics alone because jaundice is always cholangitis.
Give haematinics and review after bilirubin normalises.
Order repeat fasting lipid profile as definitive diagnosis.
Perform elective colonoscopy as first and only investigation.
explanations: Correct: painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss raises pancreatic head/biliary malignancy suspicion.
No fever/pain suggests malignant obstruction rather than acute biliary infection.
Cholestatic obstruction warrants timely imaging and tissue-directed pathway.
Lipids cannot establish site or cause of duct obstruction.
Colonoscopy does not assess pancreaticobiliary obstruction.
pearl: Courvoisier sign with painless progressive jaundice suggests malignant distal obstruction rather than gallstones.
pivot: Fever, RUQ pain and hypotension would trigger a cholangitis resuscitation and urgent drainage pathway.

steps: Investigate
LFTs, coagulation, pancreatic-protocol contrast CT and HPB/MRCP/EUS pathways.
Stage
Assess resectability and metastases with multidisciplinary HPB review; obtain tissue when indicated.
Manage jaundice
Consider ERCP stenting for cholangitis, severe symptoms or surgical/oncological planning.
Support
Nutrition, fat-soluble vitamin issues and patient-centred counselling.
management.safety: Do not delay evaluation for spontaneous jaundice resolution.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 46-year-old with known myasthenia gravis treated with pyridostigmine presents with rapidly worsening ptosis, dysphagia and breathlessness after pneumonia. Single breath count is 8, forced vital capacity low, and she has no diarrhoea, sweating or muscle fasciculations.
options: Give repeated oral pyridostigmine doses without monitoring breathing.
Admit to critical care for respiratory monitoring/support and initiate rapid immunomodulation for myasthenic crisis.
Treat as anxiety and discharge because oxygen saturation is still 97%.
Give IV magnesium to improve neuromuscular transmission.
Give high-dose benzodiazepine to control dyspnoea.
explanations: Bulbar and respiratory weakness risks airway failure; extra oral drugs do not provide adequate rescue.
Correct: infection-triggered ventilatory/bulbar failure requires airway planning plus IVIG/plasma exchange under neurology.
SpO2 may stay normal until late in neuromuscular ventilatory failure.
Magnesium can worsen myasthenic weakness.
Sedation worsens respiratory compromise.
pearl: In neuromuscular failure, respiratory muscle weakness and bulbar signs matter more than resting oxygen saturation.
pivot: Cholinergic crisis may include weakness plus muscarinic excess such as diarrhoea, salivation and fasciculations.

steps: Support airway
Urgent ICU/anaesthesia/neurology assessment, serial VC/NIF and aspiration risk assessment.
Treat trigger
Antibiotics for pneumonia chosen to avoid myasthenia-worsening agents.
Reverse crisis
IVIG or plasma exchange, immunotherapy adjustment and ventilatory support when required.
Reassess
Bulbar strength, aspiration, secretion control and medication interactions.
management.safety: Avoid drugs known to worsen MG, including certain antibiotics and magnesium.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

stem: A 42-year-old with episodic severe headache, palpitations and sweating has a 4 cm adrenal mass and plasma metanephrines four times the upper limit. He is booked for surgery in four weeks. BP between episodes is 150/90 mmHg.
ask: Which preoperative medication strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Start a beta blocker immediately without alpha blockade to control tachycardia.
Start alpha blockade first with salt/fluid optimisation; add beta blocker later only if indicated.
Give loop diuretic to cause further volume contraction before operation.
Avoid any blockade and operate urgently with usual anaesthesia.
Give calcium supplements to block catecholamine release.
explanations: Unopposed alpha-adrenergic activity can precipitate hypertensive crisis.
Correct: alpha blockade precedes beta blockade before pheochromocytoma surgery.
Patients are often volume contracted and need preoperative volume expansion.
Catecholamine release during surgery can provoke life-threatening crises.
Calcium is not a specific blockade of catecholamine physiology.
pearl: Phaeochromocytoma surgery requires alpha-adrenergic blockade before beta blockade and careful volume preparation.
pivot: A nonsecretory adrenal incidentaloma with negative endocrine testing follows different evaluation and surgical indications.

steps: Confirm biochemical diagnosis
Metanephrine evaluation and imaging guided by endocrine service.
Prepare
Alpha antagonist titration with BP monitoring, encourage appropriate salt/fluid restoration.
Control HR if needed
Add beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade; discuss anaesthetic plan.
Operate and follow
Experienced adrenal surgical team, intraoperative haemodynamic readiness and long-term surveillance.
management.safety: Never give isolated beta blockade before alpha blockade in confirmed catecholamine-secreting tumour.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.
